summary.title: A Bunch of Programming Advice I'd Give To Myself 15 Years Ago
summary.one_liner: Practical career advice for developers on fixing systemic mistakes, balancing speed against quality, debugging deeper, and asking teammates questions sooner.
keywords: writing bad code to get feedback
takeaways: Fix systemic causes of recurring bugs, such as making a subscription layer always call on the main thread, instead of patching each crash.
Match your quality bar to the context: fast shipping is fine where bugs are cheap to fix, while high-stakes financial or personal data calls for more care.
Fix bugs one layer deeper to restore invariants, and use git history when stuck on a hard bug.
Invest in debugging tools and editor/shell proficiency, and ask teammates early rather than struggling for hours.
summary.summary: The author, a developer who now feels competent, lists lessons they wish they had learned earlier, framed as advice to their younger self. Each point is illustrated with personal anecdotes from iOS, data processing, startup and Rust/React work, such as a CoreData threading fix, a memory leak traced through git history, and a logout state-ordering bug. Topics include trade-offs between quality and pace, sharpening tooling, questioning incidental complexity, building debug aids, and shipping cadence. The tone is opinionated and informal, and the author notes the advice is not universal.
